Section 3

Transmitted Flux

The goal of this section is to derive the formula for the transmitted flux measured by an observer from the physical properties of an intervening gas distribution. The structure below follows the same order as the actual calculation:

  1. In Sec. 3.1, we define the physical quantities that characterize the absorbing gas and the atomic transition responsible for the absorption.

  2. In Sec. 3.2, we relate the spectral coordinate measured by the observer to the wavelength locally associated with the photon when it passes through each point of the gas distribution.

  3. In Sec. 3.3, we use this local wavelength to determine how close the photon is to resonance with a given transition, and from this we construct the corresponding local absorption line profile.

  4. In Sec. 3.4, we integrate the local absorption contributions along the photon trajectory to obtain the optical depth.

  5. In Sec. 3.5, we convert the optical depth into transmitted flux.

  6. Finally, in Sec. 3.6, we introduce the associated flux-fluctuation field used in statistical analyses of ensembles of skewers or sightlines.

This organization helps to separate clearly the different ingredients of the problem: the physical state of the gas, the mapping between observer and absorber, the local absorption line profile, etc.

For the remaining of this section, we use the index \(i\) to denote a gas species (for example, \(\mathrm{HI}\), or \(\mathrm{SiIII}\)) and the index \(j\) to denote a specific transition associated with that species (for example Ly\(\alpha\) at \(\simeq 1215.67\,\text{\AA}\), Ly\(\beta\) at \(\simeq 1025.72\,\text{\AA}\), or SiIII transition at \(\simeq 1206.50\,\text{\AA}\)). Unless noted otherwise, the absorber is treated as a static background medium, i.e. we neglect any kind of feedback that the propagating radiation might imprint upon the gas properties.
